item.title: Your Next Insider Threat Won’t be Human: Securing AI Agents From the Outside in
item.description:
Why the controls on an AI agent have to live outside of it, and what a security operations team can do to implement and maintain those controls.

The new privileged user in your environment

Security teams spent two decades learning how to work with the people they trust most. Domain admins, DBAs, finance approvers and contractors with VPN access all get a mature playbook: verified identity, scoped access, logged activity and a fast way to revoke it all.

Today, we’re navigating the same kind of access with regard to AI agents. They read our mailboxes, query our data lakes, open tickets, push code and increasingly, act on production systems. Unlike a new hire, an agent can’t be interviewed, background-checked or made to sign an acceptable-use policy.

The industry has largely settled on one framing: AI agents are the new insider threat but that label only tells us half of the story. It tells us who to worry about, not where the controls should sit. Our argument is that the answer is a security idea from 1972, the reference monitor, and that the SOC is where it gets enforced in practice.

Why agents break the trust model we had

With traditional software, a security incident ends in a root cause. You find the vulnerable function, the misconfigured rule or the bad commit, and you fix it. The behavior lived in code we could read.

Large language models don't give us that. We can't point to the training example or the set of weights that produced a specific decision. The same prompt can produce different actions on different runs. For a defender, that removes the most basic assumption we rely on: that the system will do tomorrow what it did today.

The attack surface changes too, and computer science has an old name for this problem: the confused deputy. This is a trusted program tricked into misusing its own authority on someone else's behalf. An agent that reads a poisoned email, web page or document and then acts on hidden instructions is a confused deputy with API keys. No password is stolen and no exploit fires, which makes the agent's permissions the real blast radius, not the model's intelligence.

Where the insider analogy holds, and where it breaks

Most discussion of agents as insiders focuses on two gaps: agents have no career to lose, and they act at machine speed. Both are real. From a detection and forensics seat, though, four other differences change the work more:

Difference

Human insider

AI agent

What it means for defenders

Monoculture

One person fails on their own

Many identical copies share one weakness

Treat a working injection like a wormable bug: fix the fleet, not one instance

Replayability

Events can be reconstructed and the person interviewed

The same input can produce a different action on a rerun

Forensics must rest on recorded inputs and tool calls, not on replaying the agent

Command channel

Instructions come from a manager

Instructions arrive mixed in with the data it processes

Any content the agent reads is a potential command

Self-report

A person can be questioned and cross-checked

Its account of its reasoning may not match what it did

Evidence must come from outside the agent

The last row matters most. We can't make an agent's self-reported reasoning the basis of trust, because we don't yet know how to guarantee that reasoning is faithful. Evidence has to come from outside the agent.

Put the controls outside the model

If the model can't be fully trusted, the controls that govern it can't live inside of it. A system prompt that says "never delete production data" is a suggestion, not a control. A well-crafted injection can talk the model out of it.

Security architects solved a version of this problem in the 1970s with the reference monitor: a mechanism that checks every access request, can't be bypassed and can't be tampered with by the program it governs. For AI agents, that means separating three things: the model that reasons, the harness that orchestrates it and the policy layer that decides which actions are actually allowed.

Figure 1: Agent control architecture · enforcement outside the model

The agent can propose anything, but only the enforcement point decides what reaches real systems, and every decision lands in a log the agent can't alter.

A security playbook for AI agents

None of these controls are new. What's new is applying them consistently to a non-human actor that reasons, plans and acts.

  1. Give every agent its own identity. An agent should never run under a shared service account or a person's own credentials. It needs an identity that can be scoped, monitored, and revoked independently.

  2. Enforce least privilege on actions, not just data. Define an explicit action space: which tools, which APIs, which parameters. High-impact actions like payments, deletions or production changes need step-up approval from a human.

  3. Log everything in a place the agent can't touch. Every tool call, input, and output goes to tamper-evident storage outside the agent's reach. You should be able to reconstruct what happened without asking the agent.

  4. Never let a model grade its own work. Use a different model, a deterministic rule, or a human to verify important outcomes. Avoid depending on a single model vendor for anything critical.

  5. Red team continuously. Test prompt injection, tool misuse, data exfiltration, and edge cases, not just the happy path. Re-test every time the model, the prompt, or the tool set changes.

  6. Build a kill switch before you need it. In May 2017, WannaCry was stopped by luck. A researcher registered a nonsense domain hard-coded in the ransomware, and new infections stopped spreading because the malware checked that domain before running. Defenders didn't build that kill switch. They found it in the attacker's code, it did nothing for machines already encrypted, and later variants simply removed it. Agent fleets can't depend on that kind of luck. The stop control has to be ours, sit outside the agent, cut off its credentials and tool access mid-run, and be tested regularly, the way an EDR host isolation action is.

  7. Disclose and share incidents. When an agent misbehaves, tell the people affected, document which control failed and share the lessons with the wider community, the same way we share threat intelligence today.

  8. Persistent memory is a new risk. Agents with long-term memory can be poisoned once and stay compromised. Add memory state to "log everything" and "quarantine its outputs."

Bring agents into the Security Operations Center (SOC)

Logging alone doesn't protect anyone, as no human team can review millions of agent actions, and handing that review to another unsupervised model just adds another black box. The SOC needs to treat agent activity as a first-class telemetry source, the way it treats endpoints, identities and cloud workloads today.

In practice, that means:

  • Behavioral baselines per agent. Know which tools, data sources and destinations each agent normally uses, and alert on deviations, such as a code-review agent that starts reading the finance file share.

  • Detections for agent-specific attacks. Write rules for prompt-injection indicators, unusual tool chaining, sudden bursts of high-privilege actions and data flowing to unexpected destinations.

  • Correlation with the rest of the environment. Tie agent actions to the user, the session, the content the agent read, and the systems it touched, so an investigation can follow the full chain.

  • Response playbooks. Pause the agent, revoke its tokens, quarantine its outputs and roll back its changes, with the same speed we expect when isolating a compromised host.

The security industry can lead in this area, as we already know how to collect noisy telemetry, find the signal, and contain threats quickly. Agents are the next category of asset to protect, and the next category of actor to watch.

Trust the architecture, not the model

Models will keep getting smarter, and vendors will keep promising they're safer. Both may be true, but neither removes our responsibility for what an agent does inside our environment with our data and our credentials.

The goal isn't to find a model we can trust completely. It's to build a system that stays safe even when the model gets it wrong. Security teams have done this for people, networks, and endpoints for decades. AI agents are simply the next privileged insider, and it's time we treated them that way.

item.title: Q3 2026 Threat Update: Attackers Are Exploiting Vulnerabilities Within 3 Days (2026)
item.description:
Three days is the average time between a high-severity vulnerability becoming public and its exploitation, according to the latest Quarterly Threat Landscape Report from Rapid7. And 71% of the exploitation tracked in Q3 occurred within the first seven days.

For security teams already managing growing vulnerability backlogs, this creates a difficult question: How do you reduce exposure when attackers can exploit vulnerabilities before your next patching window?

Rapid7's Q3 2026 research brings together vulnerability intelligence, ransomware activity, APT tracking, and underground forum intelligence to show where attacker activity is concentrated.

The exploitation window has narrowed, big time

Rapid7 tracked 43 newly exploited high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities this quarter, down 7% from Q2 but still 19% higher than the same period last year.

The number of newly exploited vulnerabilities isn't growing at the same rate as disclosures. The more pressing concern is how quickly attackers exploit the vulnerabilities they choose. On average, exploitation occurred just three days after public disclosure. The report also found that 80% of tracked exploitation occurred within 14 days and 90% within 30 days.

That timeline creates a serious challenge for organizations relying on fixed remediation schedules. It also reinforces the need to distinguish between vulnerabilities that are theoretically severe and those that pose an immediate, exploitable risk.

The report examines the exploitation timeline in greater detail, including the vulnerability characteristics that make certain exposures particularly attractive to attackers.

Attackers are exploiting vulnerabilities that require no interaction

Q3's vulnerability data reveals another concerning pattern: Of the 43 newly exploited high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities tracked, 34 (79%) required no authentication or user interaction.

This provides attackers a potential path into exposed systems, no stolen credentials or malicious content interaction necessary. An internet-facing service with an exploitable vulnerability may require immediate attention, particularly when an attacker can reach it without authenticating.

This makes attack surface visibility and contextual prioritization essential. Security teams need to understand which systems are externally accessible, which vulnerabilities are actively exploited, and whether existing controls can prevent or limit compromise.

A CVSS score alone won’t give you the answers. The report explores the characteristics of exploited vulnerabilities and why understanding reachability is critical to reducing risk.

AI is taking on a more operational role in attacks

In Q3, 8% of the threat reporting tracked by Rapid7 cited AI as an operational component. The research identifies a shift from using AI primarily to help draft content or code toward supporting tactical decisions and execution within attack campaigns.

In the documented cases, human operators continued to select targets and determine objectives, but relied on AI assistance for technique selection, target assessment, and adapting when an attack step failed.

The report also examines how threat actors split malicious objectives across multiple AI sessions to evade provider safeguards. There are serious implications for detection in these findings. AI-enabled attacks also reinforce the value of monitoring and quickly adapting to attacker behavior rather than relying exclusively on known malware signatures or threat actor identities.

The report provides additional context on how AI appeared in tracked campaigns and what defenders should monitor.

The next step: Prioritize exposure before attackers exploit it

Q3's findings reveal a challenge that vulnerability counts alone can’t explain. Attackers exploited 43 newly tracked vulnerabilities this quarter, yet the average exploitation window was just three days. Meanwhile, underground forum monitoring identified 41 posts advertising RDP or network access, demonstrating continued interest in selling access to compromised environments.

Security teams must account for both the vulnerabilities attackers can exploit directly and the access they can obtain through other means.

Start by identifying externally accessible assets and the vulnerabilities affecting them. Prioritize known exploitation, unauthenticated access paths, and systems supporting critical business functions. Where immediate remediation isn't possible, assess compensating controls and detection coverage.

The latest Rapid7 Quarterly Threat Landscape Report brings together vulnerability research, ransomware intelligence, nation-state activity, and dark web monitoring to help security teams understand where threats are concentrated and what to address first. Download and read it now.

item.title: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619: Critical Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in PHP (2026)
item.description:
Overview

On October 21, 2026, the PHP project announced security releases for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP. CVE-2026-109618 can corrupt memory during out-of-memory (OOM) handling, while CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free flaw involving state retained between requests. Both have a CVSSv4 score of 9.2 and both can allow for unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) with the web worker's privileges.

CVE

CVSSv4

Description

CVE-2026-109618

9.2 (Critical)

RCE via OOM corruption

CVE-2026-109619

9.2 (Critical)

RCE via stale global state

All installations serving web requests are at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. The vendor considers mod_php the highest risk because exploitation can succeed before any application code runs.

The advisories report that a successful RCE exploit was developed during research, including achieving RCE against Apache mod_php and PHP-FPM through different attack paths. As of October 21, 2026, there are multiple indications that this research is being independently reproduced, and a viable exploit is expected to be made public soon.

Due to the extremely high deployment of PHP based web applications, exploitation in-the-wild is expected. Rapid7 recommends updating affected installations on an emergency basis, outside of normal patch cycles.

Technical overview

CVE-2026-109618: Memory corruption during OOM handling

According to the OOM advisory, PHP can abruptly abandon request processing when a memory allocation fails. If internal request data is only partly initialized, that exit can leave invalid data for request cleanup to use. Crafted multipart requests, used for forms and file uploads, can exhaust memory even when their size appears to meet PHP's configured limits. Application operations that allocate memory in response to attacker input can also trigger OOM.

Apache mod_php runs cleanup even when request startup fails, enabling the demonstrated attack before application code executes. The advisory reports RCE over HTTP with default PHP input and memory limits, including multi-worker prefork deployments. PHP-FPM terminates a worker when startup fails, preventing that particular sequence. Source analysis supports FPM susceptibility after successful startup, but the advisory reports no complete FPM exploit for this CVE. Exploit portability and reliability depend on the PHP build, extensions, frontend behavior, and memory layout.

CVE-2026-109619: Use after free across requests

PHP can reuse a worker process to handle multiple HTTP requests. The stale-state advisory describes internal state that still points to memory freed at the end of an earlier request. A later request handled by the same worker can access that stale value before normal initialization clears it. Fatal errors, including memory exhaustion and execution timeouts, can interrupt state cleanup; some nonfatal diagnostics during shutdown can also repopulate error state after it was reset.

The advisory confirms RCE against mod_php through PHP 8.5's fatal error backtrace feature, when fatal_error_backtraces is enabled (the default), where a later initialization diagnostic accesses stale backtrace state. It also confirms session lifecycle RCE against mod_php and FPM. Session upload progress, PHP's upload-tracking feature, is enabled by default and can act as an early consumer of stale session or decoder state before normal initialization; reaching this consumer does not itself require an application call to session_start().

The validated FPM session path requires a suitable application operation to leave state behind after successful startup, followed by a fatal error and another request that consumes the stale state through session upload progress. Both requests must reach the same worker. Multiple workers and worker recycling can reduce success per request, but do not eliminate the condition.

Mitigation guidance

PHP has released fixes for both vulnerabilities. Organizations should prioritize updating to the appropriate fixed release or a vendor package containing both complete patches. The PHP advisories list these affected and fixed versions:

  • PHP 8.2 releases before 8.2.35: Update to 8.2.35

  • PHP 8.3 releases before 8.3.36: Update to 8.3.36

  • PHP 8.4 releases before 8.4.27: Update to 8.4.27

  • PHP 8.5 releases before 8.5.12: Update to 8.5.12

Linux distributions and long-term support vendors received patches in advance; check your vendor for updated packages. PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive routine upstream updates. For this incident, PHP has supplied limited source backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1. Organizations running older branches should obtain a vendor fix, use the source backports described in the PHP announcement, or upgrade to a supported version. PHP also warns that rpms.remirepo.net will not have updates on October 21, 2026, and urges its users to switch to distribution packages or build from source.

Note that an update containing both complete fixes is the only complete remediation. 

PHP's temporary configuration measures reduce exposure to specific paths and require careful deployment:

  • For the OOM issue, enforce memory_limit=-1 administratively, such as through FPM pool or Apache configuration that applications cannot override. This disables PHP's per-request memory cap and removes the predictable PHP-limit failure used by the confirmed exploit. An underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path. Restart every worker and verify that no pool, directory, or application setting restores a finite limit.

  • For the session lifecycle path, set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in php.ini, an FPM pool, or server configuration that applies before request parsing, then restart every worker. Application-level ini_set() and FPM .user.ini are too late. This addresses the confirmed session paths only.

  • On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 administratively and restart every worker. This addresses the confirmed fatal backtrace path only; other retained state remains a concern.

Disabling PHP's memory cap makes independent resource controls particularly important. PHP recommends post_max_size=8M where uploads are unnecessary or post_max_size=32M where they are needed, with upload_max_filesize below that limit. At the frontend, bound decoded request size, input and multipart counts, headers per part, and nesting depth, including requests without a usable Content-Length. If the application does not use multipart data, block those requests before they reach PHP.

Container or cgroup memory limits are also incomplete: allocation failures remain possible, and enforcement can kill the master process and all workers unless workers are isolated. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, which can trigger the vulnerable allocation-failure path.

For stale-state exposure, correct invalid or deprecated per-request settings and attacker-reachable fatal errors or timeouts. Hiding diagnostics through error_reporting, display_errors, log_errors, or @ does not prevent stale-state access. The absence of relevant log entries is not proof that an installation is safe.

For the latest mitigation guidance, refer to PHP's OOM corruption advisory and stale global state advisory.

Rapid7 customers

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 with remote unauthenticated vulnerability checks now available in a dedicated release, which followed the normal daily October 21 content release.

Velociraptor

A Velociraptor Artifact Generic.Applications.PHPInventory is available to inventory PHP installations on Windows, Linux and macOS for remediation scoping. This artifact allows for the collection of package versions, common binary and module paths, and running PHP processes.

Updates

  • October 21, 2026: Initial publication.

  • October 21, 2026: Updated to reflect availability of vulnerability checks.

Fatal errors, including memory exhaustion and execution timeouts, can interrupt state cleanup; some nonfatal diagnostics during shutdown can also repopulate error state after it was reset.

The advisory confirms RCE against mod_php through PHP 8.5's fatal error backtrace feature, when fatal_error_backtraces is enabled (the default), where a later initialization diagnostic accesses stale backtrace state. It also confirms session lifecycle RCE against mod_php and FPM. Session upload progress, PHP's upload-tracking feature, is enabled by default and can act as an early consumer of stale session or decoder state before normal initialization; reaching this consumer does not itself require an application call to session_start().

The validated FPM session path requires a suitable application operation to leave state behind after successful startup, followed by a fatal error and another request that consumes the stale state through session upload progress. Both requests must reach the same worker. Multiple workers and worker recycling can reduce success per request, but do not eliminate the condition.

Mitigation guidance

PHP has released fixes for both vulnerabilities. Organizations should prioritize updating to the appropriate fixed release or a vendor package containing both complete patches. The PHP advisories list these affected and fixed versions:

  • PHP 8.2 releases before 8.2.35: Update to 8.2.35

  • PHP 8.3 releases before 8.3.36: Update to 8.3.36

  • PHP 8.4 releases before 8.4.27: Update to 8.4.27

  • PHP 8.5 releases before 8.5.12: Update to 8.5.12

Linux distributions and long-term support vendors received patches in advance; check your vendor for updated packages. PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive routine upstream updates. For this incident, PHP has supplied limited source backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1. Organizations running older branches should obtain a vendor fix, use the source backports described in the PHP announcement, or upgrade to a supported version. PHP also warns that rpms.remirepo.net will not have updates on October 21, 2026, and urges its users to switch to distribution packages or build from source.

Note that an update containing both complete fixes is the only complete remediation. 

PHP's temporary configuration measures reduce exposure to specific paths and require careful deployment:

  • For the OOM issue, enforce memory_limit=-1 administratively, such as through FPM pool or Apache configuration that applications cannot override. This disables PHP's per-request memory cap and removes the predictable PHP-limit failure used by the confirmed exploit. An underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path. Restart every worker and verify that no pool, directory, or application setting restores a finite limit.

  • For the session lifecycle path, set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in php.ini, an FPM pool, or server configuration that applies before request parsing, then restart every worker. Application-level ini_set() and FPM .user.ini are too late. This addresses the confirmed session paths only.

  • On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 administratively and restart every worker. This addresses the confirmed fatal backtrace path only; other retained state remains a concern.

Disabling PHP's memory cap makes independent resource controls particularly important. PHP recommends post_max_size=8M where uploads are unnecessary or post_max_size=32M where they are needed, with upload_max_filesize below that limit. At the frontend, bound decoded request size, input and multipart counts, headers per part, and nesting depth, including requests without a usable Content-Length. If the application does not use multipart data, block those requests before they reach PHP.

Container or cgroup memory limits are also incomplete: allocation failures remain possible, and enforcement can kill the master process and all workers unless workers are isolated. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, which can trigger the vulnerable allocation-failure path.

For stale-state exposure, correct invalid or deprecated per-request settings and attacker-reachable fatal errors or timeouts. Hiding diagnostics through error_reporting, display_errors, log_errors, or @ does not prevent stale-state access. The absence of relevant log entries is not proof that an installation is safe.

For the latest mitigation guidance, refer to PHP's OOM corruption advisory and stale global state advisory.
